content: 1. The process of real-time calibration of lessons learned during an ongoing public health response is essential. This can be achieved through regular meetings, such as weekly epidemiology or outbreak review sessions, to assess and refine response strategies. 2. Recommendations derived from Early Action Reviews (EAR) can be instrumental in shaping outbreak response plans, incident action plans, or other response planning tools. 3. To integrate the EAR into existing meetings, it is recommended to include agenda items that focus on discussing the event, evaluating the timeliness of the response, identifying bottlenecks and enablers, and determining remedial actions. 4. A sample 20-minute agenda for an EAR includes: 5 minutes to discuss the event background, key milestones, and timeliness metrics. 5 minutes to identify bottlenecks and enablers in detection, notification, and early response. 10 minutes to prioritize remedial actions, address remaining early response actions, and assign responsibilities for immediate actions. 5. Data for EAR discussions can be summarized using the Event Review Template (Tool 2), which facilitates structured analysis and presentation of findings. 6. Emergency Operations Centers (EOCs) or equivalent Incident Management Systems (IMS) are ideal hosts for EAR exercises due to their established roles in data collection, analysis, decision-making, and coordination. 7. EARs can be conducted in various settings, such as dedicated EOC meetings for ongoing public health threats or integrated into routine epidemiology or outbreak review meetings held weekly or monthly. 8. The EAR approach has been successfully used in countries like Uganda during the Sudan Ebola virus disease outbreak in Mubende. The Uganda Ministry of Health and the Infectious Diseases Institute implemented a rapid performance improvement strategy aligned with the 7-1-7 target, using the Event Review Template to assess performance and address bottlenecks. 9. Immediate actions taken during the Uganda Ebola response included securing funding for contact tracing and improving isolation facilities. Long-term actions, such as nationwide training in integrated disease surveillance and response for private healthcare providers, were incorporated into national planning. 10. The Post-EAR Action Tracker (Tool 3) is used to monitor the implementation status of remedial actions. It categorizes progress into five stages: completed, in progress, stuck, waiting, and deferred. 11. Routine monitoring of remedial actions during meetings ensures accountability and timely completion, supporting performance improvement efforts. 12. Some actions initially prioritized for immediate implementation may remain incomplete and need to be integrated into longer-term planning processes, such as a National Action Plan for Health Security (NAPHS). 13. EAR findings can be synthesized into periodic reports to identify patterns and recurring bottlenecks across multiple events. This supports prioritization of funding and implementation to address systemic issues. 14. The Synthesis Report Template (Tool 4) can be used to develop high-level summaries of lessons learned across multiple events, aiding in national planning and advocacy efforts. 15. EAR outputs can be incorporated into intra-action reviews (IAR) and after-action reviews (AAR) to provide a comprehensive overview of performance and inform future improvements. 16. The EAR approach aligns with the 7-1-7 target, which emphasizes completing seven key early response actions within seven days of notification. This framework ensures rapid detection, notification, and response to public health threats. 17. The EAR methodology promotes a virtuous cycle of accountability and advocacy by providing stakeholders with clear progress metrics and demonstrating the impact of investments in public health systems. 18. Supporting tools for conducting EARs, including templates and trackers, are available for download and are periodically updated to meet evolving needs. 19. The date of emergence of a health event is determined based on epidemiological data and may change as more information becomes available. This date is critical for understanding the timeline of an outbreak. 20. The date of detection refers to when a public health event is first recorded in any system, while the date of notification is when the event is reported to a public health authority responsible for taking action. 21. The completion date of early response actions is the latest date on which any of the seven early response actions is completed. Not all actions may apply to every public health event, depending on the risk assessment.
